name: Mirizzi syndrome
aliases: extrinsic bile duct compression by cystic duct stone

reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Obstructive jaundice caused by extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck
Presents with jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and often features of cholangitis, mimicking choledocholithiasis or a biliary malignancy
Classified by the presence and extent of a cholecystobiliary fistula, which develops as chronic pressure erodes between the gallbladder and the bile duct
Requires a low threshold of suspicion, as it is frequently unrecognised before surgery and increases the risk of bile duct injury
MRCP is valuable for demonstrating the impacted stone, the level of compression, and any fistula
There is an association with gallbladder carcinoma, so malignancy should be considered during evaluation
Management depends on type: cholecystectomy for simple compression, and biliary reconstruction or repair when a fistula is present, with ERCP useful for decompression, stone clearance, and stenting
reference.pathophysiology: Mirizzi syndrome arises when a gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct or the neck (Hartmann's pouch) of the gallbladder, usually where the cystic duct runs a long parallel course alongside the common hepatic duct. The stone and the surrounding inflammatory reaction compress the adjacent common hepatic duct extrinsically, obstructing bile flow and causing jaundice. Persistent pressure and chronic inflammation can erode the wall separating the gallbladder from the bile duct, producing a cholecystobiliary fistula of varying size; in advanced disease the stone may migrate into the common duct. The dense inflammation and distorted anatomy in Calot's triangle obscure normal landmarks and predispose to iatrogenic bile duct injury during cholecystectomy.
additionalInvestigations: MRI with MRCP to localise the impacted stone, level of obstruction, and any fistula
Abdominal ultrasound to detect gallstones, a contracted gallbladder, and duct dilatation
ERCP for diagnosis, biliary decompression, stone clearance, and stenting
Liver function tests to characterise the cholestatic picture
Serum CA 19-9 and cross-sectional imaging when malignancy is a concern
Endoscopic ultrasound to further assess the stone and exclude a mass
redFlags: Ascending cholangitis with fever, rigors, and sepsis
Features suggesting coexisting gallbladder carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma
A large cholecystobiliary fistula complicating operative management
Rising bilirubin with worsening liver function
Intraoperative loss of normal anatomical landmarks in Calot's triangle
reference.prognosis: With timely recognition and appropriate surgery the outlook is generally good, but the syndrome carries a higher risk of bile duct injury and operative complications than routine gallstone disease, and the associated gallbladder carcinoma, if present, worsens prognosis considerably.
pitfalls: Failing to anticipate the diagnosis preoperatively, increasing the risk of common duct injury during cholecystectomy
Attempting a straightforward laparoscopic cholecystectomy in dense inflammation without recognising distorted anatomy
Overlooking a cholecystobiliary fistula that alters the required operation
Inadequate biliary decompression in the presence of cholangitis
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Reviews of the diagnosis and surgical management of Mirizzi syndrome
management: Definitive treatment is cholecystectomy with clearance of the impacted stone; a fistula-free duct allows standard cholecystectomy, whereas a cholecystobiliary fistula requires subtotal cholecystectomy with fistula closure or biliary reconstruction such as choledochoplasty or hepaticojejunostomy
Preoperative ERCP for biliary decompression, stone extraction and temporary stent placement to relieve obstructive jaundice and cholangitis before surgery
Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes when cholangitis is present, with correction of coagulopathy from cholestasis
Intraoperative cholangiography and careful dissection of Calot's triangle to define the distorted anatomy and minimise the heightened risk of iatrogenic bile duct injury
Actively exclude coexisting gallbladder carcinoma during evaluation and submit the resected gallbladder for histology
Refer to a hepatobiliary surgical unit for complex fistulating disease, with a low threshold for conversion from laparoscopic to open surgery
